- The domain of the 2nd component $3$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

- The domain of the 3rd component $\sqrt{{t}^{2}+2}$ is $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

The intersection is illustrated in the diagram below.

:question/id #uuid "751ef612-b871-5a13-b5db-9f9345197dd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-80813" :question/problem "Which of the following are subsets of ${Q}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative rational numbers)?

I. ${Z}^{-}$ (the set of negative integers)

II. $N$

III. ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative integers)" :question/worked-solution "$A$ is a subset of $B$ if every element of $A$ is an element of $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect the given choices.

- ${Z}^{-}$ is not a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ For example, $-1\in {Z}^{-}$ but $-1\notin {Q}_{0}^{+}.$

- $N$ is a subset of ${Q}^{+}.$ Indeed, every natural number is also a positive rational number.

- ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ is a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ Indeed, every positive integer is also a positive rational number. Notice also that  $0$ is in both  ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ and ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III  only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eb49e450-3c82-56fd-b065-47510e61dd32"] :db/ensure $$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186240618 :answer-field/correct "answer-d162144b-b4a5-51ba-9d97-5bb11fc0f3da" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fb4e1fb8-de8c-57db-9ec1-0460004b76fc" "answer-bd06c2c2-b428-571e-8760-4cbeaa7dcc7a" "answer-d89d63a8-9075-5e20-bc27-e5a349ddda2d" "answer-d162144b-b4a5-51ba-9d97-5bb11fc0f3da" "answer-814bed9d-2cbb-5df1-896f-d87d4713951f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fb4e1fb8-de8c-57db-9ec1-0460004b76fc" :answer/id #uuid "fb4e1fb8-de8c-57db-9ec1-0460004b76fc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{1,16\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bd06c2c2-b428-571e-8760-4cbeaa7dcc7a" :answer/id #uuid "bd06c2c2-b428-571e-8760-4cbeaa7dcc7a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d89d63a8-9075-5e20-bc27-e5a349ddda2d" :answer/id #uuid "d89d63a8-9075-5e20-bc27-e5a349ddda2d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{2,4,8,16\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d162144b-b4a5-51ba-9d97-5bb11fc0f3da" :answer/id #uuid "d162144b-b4a5-51ba-9d97-5bb11fc0f3da" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{6,10,12,14\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-814bed9d-2cbb-5df1-896f-d87d4713951f" :answer/id #uuid "814bed9d-2cbb-5df1-896f-d87d4713951f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{6,12\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186362318 :question/problem "![](images/6b/6b9b15bd3c8cda84156d5461fb9f80f892a1dba26151cc37d381757f9f659fa1.png)

Consider the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y)$ where the graph of $f(y)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $y=-3$ is a node.

II. $y=2$ is a sink.

III. $y=2$ is a source." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083393 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-856c86c0-9a1d-541f-bee9-93df07ee1d90"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-856c86c0-9a1d-541f-bee9-93df07ee1d90" :question/id #uuid "856c86c0-9a1d-541f-bee9-93df07ee1d90" :question/math-academy-id "q-102697" :question/problem "A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6t-2$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=3\,\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-2)\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =3(1)^{2}-2(1)+C \\ -1 & =3-2+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{t}^{2}-2t-2.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=3\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =3(3)^{2}-2(3)-2 \\  & =27-6-2 \\  & =19\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $19\,\text{m/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ba55cb3c-40db-5e24-bdf4-2cb74a217cfc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ba55cb3c-40db-5e24-bdf4-2cb74a217cfc" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba55cb3c-40db-5e24-bdf4-2cb74a217cfc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" :answer-field/choices ["answer-12fdb718-5b20-5e1f-bedc-4a924bf08daa" "answer-df95a53e-89cb-595f-b895-96655799381a" "answer-28abf313-cb2f-5450-b131-e9fc73d1c015" "answer-0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" "answer-d2363bc7-c793-5cae-a7a0-fdb45b1f9144"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-12fdb718-5b20-5e1f-bedc-4a924bf08daa" :answer/id #uuid "12fdb718-5b20-5e1f-bedc-4a924bf08daa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-df95a53e-89cb-595f-b895-96655799381a" :answer/id #uuid "df95a53e-89cb-595f-b895-96655799381a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "11\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28abf313-cb2f-5450-b131-e9fc73d1c015" :answer/id #uuid "28abf313-cb2f-5450-b131-e9fc73d1c015" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" :answer/id #uuid "0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "19\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2363bc7-c793-5cae-a7a0-fdb45b1f9144" :answer/id #uuid "d2363bc7-c793-5cae-a7a0-fdb45b1f9144" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186241023 :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\ -2s+5t=1 \\ -s-t=4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\ t=-1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-1.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-4t & =1 \\ s-4(-1) & =1 \\ s+4 & =1 \\ s & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-3,\,t=-1,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-3b-c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-3)\cdot (-1)=3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186338872 :question/problem "Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

II. $N$

III. ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative integers)" :question/worked-solution "$A$ is a subset of $B$ if every element of $A$ is an element of $B.$

- ${Z}^{-}$ is not a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ For example, $-1\in {Z}^{-}$ but $-1\notin {Q}_{0}^{+}.$

- $N$ is a subset of ${Q}^{+}.$ Indeed, every natural number is also a positive rational number.

- ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ is a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ Indeed, every positive integer is also a positive rational number. Notice also that  $0$ is in both  ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ and ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$

If the particle has velocity $v=-1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=3\,\text{s}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-2)\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =3(1)^{2}-2(1)+C \\ -1 & =3-2+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{t}^{2}-2t-2.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=3\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =3(3)^{2}-2(3)-2 \\  & =27-6-2 \\  & =19\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $19\,\text{m/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ba55cb3c-40db-5e24-bdf4-2cb74a217cfc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ba55cb3c-40db-5e24-bdf4-2cb74a217cfc" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba55cb3c-40db-5e24-bdf4-2cb74a217cfc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" :answer-field/choices ["answer-12fdb718-5b20-5e1f-bedc-4a924bf08daa" "answer-df95a53e-89cb-595f-b895-96655799381a" "answer-28abf313-cb2f-5450-b131-e9fc73d1c015" "answer-0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" "answer-d2363bc7-c793-5cae-a7a0-fdb45b1f9144"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-12fdb718-5b20-5e1f-bedc-4a924bf08daa" :answer/id #uuid "12fdb718-5b20-5e1f-bedc-4a924bf08daa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-df95a53e-89cb-595f-b895-96655799381a" :answer/id #uuid "df95a53e-89cb-595f-b895-96655799381a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "11\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28abf313-cb2f-5450-b131-e9fc73d1c015" :answer/id #uuid "28abf313-cb2f-5450-b131-e9fc73d1c015" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" :answer/id #uuid "0de2057b-88f3-5eae-a4be-76fa3eb87360" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "19\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2363bc7-c793-5cae-a7a0-fdb45b1f9144" :answer/id #uuid "d2363bc7-c793-5cae-a7a0-fdb45b1f9144" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20\,\text{m/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186241023 :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\ -2s+5t=1 \\ -s-t=4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\ t=-1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-1.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-4t & =1 \\ s-4(-1) & =1 \\ s+4 & =1 \\ s & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-3,\,t=-1,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-3b-c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-3)\cdot (-1)=3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186338872 :question/problem "Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

:question/problem "Which of the following are subsets of ${Q}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative rational numbers)?

I. ${Z}^{-}$ (the set of negative integers)

II. $N$

III. ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ (the set of non-negative integers)"] ["question-751ef612-b871-5a13-b5db-9f9345197dd4" :question/worked-solution "$A$ is a subset of $B$ if every element of $A$ is an element of $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect the given choices.

- ${Z}^{-}$ is not a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ For example, $-1\in {Z}^{-}$ but $-1\notin {Q}_{0}^{+}.$

- $N$ is a subset of ${Q}^{+}.$ Indeed, every natural number is also a positive rational number.

- ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ is a subset of ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$ Indeed, every positive integer is also a positive rational number. Notice also that  $0$ is in both  ${Z}_{0}^{+}$ and ${Q}_{0}^{+}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III  only"."] ["question-751ef612-b871-5a13-b5db-9f9345197dd4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] Consider the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y)$ where the graph of $f(y)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true?

I. $y=-3$ is a node.

II. $y=2$ is a sink.

If the particle has velocity $v=-1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=3\,\text{s}.$"] ["question-856c86c0-9a1d-541f-bee9-93df07ee1d90" :question/worked-solution "First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-2)\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =3(1)^{2}-2(1)+C \\ -1 & =3-2+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{t}^{2}-2t-2.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=3\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =3(3)^{2}-2(3)-2 \\  & =27-6-2 \\  & =19\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

\\\\ z=7-6t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nfor $t\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line." :question/worked-solution "First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y \\\\ z\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2+4t \\\\ -3+5t \\\\ 7-6t\\end{aligned}] \\\\ [\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y \\\\ z\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -3 \\\\ 7\\end{aligned}]+[\\begin{aligned}4t \\\\ 5t \\\\ -6t\\end{aligned}] \\\\ [\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y \\\\ z\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -3 \\\\ 7\\end{aligned}]+t[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 5 \\\\ -6\\end{aligned}] \\\\ r & =[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -3 \\\\ 7\\end{aligned}]+t[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 5 \\\\ -6\\end{aligned}],\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $t\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ).$\n\nThis implies that the given line passes through the point $P(2,-3,7)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,-6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by\n\n$$\n\\frac{x-2}{4}=\\frac{y-(-3)}{5}=\\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\\,t\\in (-\\infty ,\\infty ).\n$$\n\nSimplifying, we the affirmative case, find the value of $s\\cdot t$ from the decomposition $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\\\ s[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ -2 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}]+t[\\begin{aligned}-4 \\\\ 5 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}] & =[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 4\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have the following system of equations:\n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\\\ -2s+5t=1 \\\\ -s-t=4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & [\\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\\\ -2 & 5 & 1 \\\\ -1 & -1 & 4\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\\\ -1 & -1 & 4\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\\\ 0 & -5 & 5\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\\\ 0 & -5 & 5\\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we have the system\n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}s-4t=1 \\\\ t=-1 \\\\ 0=0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the second equation, we get\n\n$$\nt=-1.\n$$\n\nSubstituting into the first equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}s-4t & =1 \\\\ s-4(-1) & =1 \\\\ s+4 & =1 \\\\ s & =-3.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince we found a solution $s=-3,\\,t=-1,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have\n\n$$\nu=-3b-c.\n$$\n\nFinally, $s\\cdot t=(-3)\\cdot (-1)=3.$"} {:db/id 17592186241024 :question/id #uuid "The **difference** of two sets $A$ and $B,$ denoted by $A \\setminus B$ or $A - B,$ is the set of all elements belonging to $A$ and *not* belonging to $B.$\n\nFor example, consider the sets $A = \\{ a,b,c \\}$ and $B = \\{ b, d, e \\}.$ We can represent these sets using a Venn diagram, as follows:\n\n![](images/4a/4a2d3be8c64b5527dcb37ac68d99cd1e36009725d0847597c5bbd417bbd5f7ad.png)\n\nThe difference $A \\setminus B$ consists of all the elements that are in $A$ but not $B.$ To represent $A \\setminus B,$ we will shade in all the area that is contained within $A$ but not $B.$\n\n![](images/49/49743d4647817294c2287bc15a496fb5d6c73070ed52cfd8934d1babe93c1b25.png)\n\nThe elements $a$ and $c$ are contained in $A$ but not $B.$ Therefore,\n\n$$\nA \\setminus B = A - B = \\{ a,c \\}.\n$$\n\n**Note:** The difference can be defined using set-builder notation as follows:\n\n$$\nA \\setminus B = A - B = \\{ x \\mid x \\in A \\text { and } x \\notin B \\}\n$$\n\nThe condition \"$x \\in A \\text { and } x \\notin B$\" means that $x$ must belong to $A$ but $x$ must *not* belong to $B.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48529a2b-cc59-57e8-8624-78fd4339f88c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4333 {:db/id 17592186158129 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158480 :tutorial/content "Although Venn diagrams can be useful to visualize differences, we do not have to draw a Venn diagram every time we wish to compute a difference.\n\nFor example, let's again consider the sets $A = \\{ a,b,c \\}$ and $B = \\{ b, d, e \\}.$ This time, we will compute the difference $A \\setminus B$ without using a Venn diagram. We just need to find all the elements that are in $A$ but not $B.$\n\nSo, we will go through the elements of $A$ and check if each element is also in $B.$ Remember that we are looking for elements that are *not* in $B.$\n\n- For the element $a \\in A,$ we have $a \\not\\in B. \\quad \\color{green}\\checkmark$\n\n- For the element $b \\in A,$ we have $b \\in B. \\quad \\color{red}\\times$\n\n- For the element $c \\in A,$ we have $c \\not\\in B. \\quad \\color{green}\\checkmark$\n\nThe elements of $A$ that are not in $B$ are $a$ and $c.$\n\nTherefore, the difference is\n\n$$\nA \\setminus B = A - B = \\{ a,c \\}.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "14afef0e-fec6-5cdf-82c4-98391973df49" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4342 :tutorial/title "Differences Without Venn Diagrams"} :step/id #uuid Then,\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[aX] = a^2\\textrm{Var}[X].\n$$\n\nSo, for example, if we know that $\\textrm{Var}[X] = 2,$ then\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Var}[3X] & ={3}^{2}\\cdot \\text{Var}[X] \\\\  & =9\\cdot \\text{Var}[X] \\\\  & =9\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =18.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Var}[-4X] & =(-4)^{2}\\cdot \\text{Var}[X] \\\\  & =16\\cdot \\text{Var}[X] \\\\  & =16\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =32.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** To understand why we have to square the constant when we factor it outside the variance, it's helpful to remember that the variance is defined as the expected *squared* deviation from the mean:\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Var}[X] = \\textrm E [ (X - \\textrm E[X])^2 ]\n$$\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Var}[aX] & =\\text{E}[(aX-\\text{E}[aX])^{2}] \\\\  & =\\text{E}[(aX-a\\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\\\  & =\\text{E}[{a}^{2}(X-\\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\\\  & ={a}^{2}\\text{E}[(X-\\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\\\  & ={a}^{2}\\text{Var}[X].\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d33b6982-066e-5c82-8138-0283ad8dccbb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5459 :tutorial/title "The Variance of a Scaled Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "55f9fd86-1f4a-5f2c-b7c2-a60113a4a9e8" :step/math-academy-id 33966 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162972}} {:db/id 17592186162976 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163275 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ is a random variable and $a$ and $b$ are constants. domain of a vector-valued function $\\mathbf f(t)$ is the set of values of $t$ for which the function is well-defined. \n\nA function is well-defined at some value $t = t_0$ if all its component functions are defined at $t_0.$ Thus, the domain of $\\mathbf f$ is the *intersection* of the domains of its component functions.\n\nLet's find the domain of the following function:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{f}(t) = \\dfrac{1}{3+t} \\: \\mathbf i + t^2 \\: \\mathbf j + \\sqrt{-t} \\: \\mathbf k\n$$\n\nFirst, we find the domains of the component functions:\n\n- The domain of $\\dfrac{1}{3+t}$ is $t \\in (-\\infty,-3) \\cup (-3,\\infty).$\n\n- The domain of $t^2$ is $t \\in (-\\infty,\\infty).$\n\n- The domain of $\\sqrt{-t}$ is $t \\in (-\\infty, 0].$\n\nTo find the domain of $\\mathbf{f},$ we need the intersection of the component functions' domains. This intersection is illustrated in the diagram below.\n\n![](images/7c/7cf7270cc873e9de1fedb7bd413bba1f9ed1f7cd604b3ae640d32d9e0b41bdef.png)\n\nTherefore, the domain of the function $\\mathbf{f}(t)$ is $t \\in (-\\infty,-3) \\cup (-3,0].$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d01e4be3-25c3-5922-9f88-c8eb7538e62e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7628 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid the domain of $\\mathbf f$ is the *intersection* of the domains of its component functions.\n\nLet's find the domain of the following function:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{f}(t) = \\dfrac{1}{3+t} \\: \\mathbf i + t^2 \\: \\mathbf j + \\sqrt{-t} \\: \\mathbf k\n$$\n\nFirst, we find the domains of the component functions:\n\n- The domain of $\\dfrac{1}{3+t}$ is $t \\in (-\\infty,-3) \\cup (-3,\\infty).$\n\n- The domain of $t^2$ is $t \\in (-\\infty,\\infty).$\n\n- The domain of $\\sqrt{-t}$ is $t \\in (-\\infty, 0].$\n\nTo find the domain of $\\mathbf{f},$ we need the intersection of the component functions' domains. two sets $A$ and $B,$ if every element of $A$ is an element of $B,$ we say that $A$ is a **subset** of $B,$ and we write \n\n$$\nA \\subseteq B.\n$$\n\nFor example, consider the following sets:\n\n$$\nA = \\{ {\\color{blue}{1}},{\\color{blue}{3}} \\}, \\qquad B = \\{ 1,2,3\\}, \\qquad C=\\{1,2,{\\color{red}4}\\}\n$$\n\n \n\nNotice that *every* element of $A$ is also an element of $B{:}$\n\n$$\n{\\color{blue}{1}}\\in B, \\qquad {\\color{blue}{3}}\\in B\n$$\n\nTherefore, $A$ is a subset of $B,$ and we write $A \\subseteq B.$\n\nWe can visualize the sets $A$ and $B$ as shown element $0\\in A.$ We can either include it or not include it in a new subset.\n\n- If we don't include $0$ in $\\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\\{ \\}},$ we are left with the empty set \\}},$ we get the set $\\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{\\{0\\}}.$ Next, we consider the element $1\\in A.$ We can either include it or not include it in a new subset:\n\n- If we don't include $1$ in $\\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{\\{0\\}},$ we are left with $\\bbox[2pt,Thistle]{\\{0\\}}.$\n\n- If we include $1$ in $\\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{\\{0\\}},$ we get $\\bbox[2pt,Thistle]{\\{0,1\\}}.$\n\nFinally, the list of all subsets is shown in the last column:\n\n$$\n\\bbox[2pt,Thistle]{\\{\\}},\\quad \\: \\bbox[2pt,Thistle]{\\{0\\}},\\quad \\: \\bbox[2pt,Thistle]{\\{1\\}},\\quad \\: \\bbox[2pt,Thistle]{\\{0,1\\}}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "daebe910-6059-595b-a45a-fc890a9b1b53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8244 :tutorial/title "Listing All the Subsets of a Set"} :step/id #uuid "2e361262-f159-54e6-a942-659d5017ac7b" :step/math-academy-id 152764 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055558}} {:db/id 17592186055558 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056056 :tutorial/content "Recall that the natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and real and complex numbers can be arranged in the following hierarchical diagram.\n\n![](images/66/66260e4c239137cd30453d9335256fd7d84e93a197612d670c19d97e417bd2f0.png)\n\nIn other words, $\\mathbb{N}$ is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{Z},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{Q},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{R},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{C}.$ We can write this symbolically as follows:\n\n$$\n\\mathbb{N} \\subseteq \\mathbb{Z} \\subseteq \\mathbb{Q} \\subseteq \\mathbb{R} \\subseteq \\mathbb{C}\n$$\n\nSince none of these sets are equivalent, we can also write\n\n$$\n\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z} \\subset \\mathbb{Q} \\subset \\mathbb{R} \\subset \\mathbb{C}.\n$$\n\nSome restricted or extended special sets are subsets of others. For example:\n\n- $\\mathbb N$ is the set of natural numbers, and $\\mathbb N_0$ is the set of natural numbers *and* zero. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\mathbb N\\subset \\mathbb N_0.\n$$\n\n- $\\mathbb Z$ is the set of integers, $\\mathbb Z^+$ is the set of positive integers (equivalent to $\\mathbb N$), and $\\mathbb Z^+_0$ is the set of positive integers and zero (equivalent to $\\mathbb N_0$). Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\mathbb Z^+\\subset  \\mathbb Z_0^+ \\subset \\mathbb Z.\n$$\n\n- $\\mathbb Q^+$ is the set of positive rational numbers, $\\mathbb R^+$ is the set of positive real numbers, and $\\mathbb R$ is the set of real numbers. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\mathbb Q^+\\subset  \\mathbb R^+ \\subset \\mathbb R.\n$$\n\nHowever, note that, for example, $\\mathbb Q \\not\\subset  \\mathbb R^+,$ since $0\\in\\mathbb Q$ yet $0\\notin \\mathbb R^+.$\n\nFrom these basic inclusions, we can now deduce some subset relationships for other special numerical sets. For example, recall that [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] represents the set of all non-negative integers. \n\n* Obviously, [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] is a proper subset of [math]\\mathbb{Z}[/math] since all the elements of [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] are integers but there are some integers, say, [math]-1,[/math] that does not belong to [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+.[/math] So, [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+ \\subset \\mathbb{Z}.[/math]\n\n* On the other hand, [math]\\mathbb{N}[/math] is a proper subset of [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] since all natural number lie in [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] but [math]0 \\notin \\mathbb{N}.[/math] So, [math]\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z}_0^+.[/math]\n\nTherefore, we have [math]\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z}_0^+ \\subset \\mathbb{Z}.[/math]" :tutorial/id Can't we just let the universal set be the set of everything?\n\nThe answer is no. If we don't specify a well-defined universal set, we encounter a nonsensical situation called **Russell's paradox.**\n\nFirst, suppose there exists a set $\\Omega$ that contains absolutely everything, including every mathematical object, every thought, every book, every person, animal, cell, and star in the universe, past, present, or future. \n\nRussell's paradox originates from the following idea:\n\n> *Define $S$ as the set that contains all sets that are not elements of themselves.*\n> \n> \n> $$\n> S = \\{A\\in \\Omega\\,:\\, A\\notin A\\}\n> $$\n\nMost sets you can think of are elements of $S.$ For example, the set $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}$ is in $S$ because $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}\\notin \\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$ \n\nIt takes a bit of thought to find sets that *aren't* members of $S.$ Such sets do exist, although typical examples are somewhat abstract: \n\n- The set containing all possible sets.\n\n- The set containing all possible thoughts.\n\n- The set $X,$ given by\n\n$$\nX = \\Big\\{\\underbrace{\\big\\{ \\left\\{\\{\\ldots \\}\\right\\}\\big\\}}_{X}\\Big\\}.\n$$\n\nHowever, what about $S$ itself? Is $S$ an element of $S?$ There are only two possibilities:\n\n- If $S\\in S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\notin S.$ But this is a contradiction because we cannot have $S\\in S$ *and* $S\\notin S.$\n\n- If $S\\notin S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we must have that $S\\in S.$ But this leads to the same contradiction as before!\n\nThe only way to resolve this is to conclude that $S\\notin \\Omega,$ but this is also a contradiction since $\\Omega$ contains absolutely everything!  So, there is no consistent answer to the question of whether $S$ itself is an element of $S.$ This is Russell's paradox, and when it was discovered, it shook the foundations of mathematics to its very core.\n\nThe issue, unknown to mathematicians until later, is that the object [math]S[/math] is not a set. If it were, Russell's paradox would not occur since we should always be able to determine whether an object is a member of a set or not.\n\nLater, it was realized that if a set is defined using a predicate, we should ensure that all sets involved are subsets of some larger set $U$ (i.e., a universal set) where we can always determine which elements are members of $U$ and which are not, at least in principle.\n\nTo see how this resolves Russell's paradox, suppose $U$ is a universal set. Let's refine our definition of $S$ as follows:\n\n$$\nS = \\{A\\subseteq U\\,:\\,A\\notin A\\}\n$$\n\nWe'll assume $S$ is a set, so $S\\subseteq U$ for some well-defined $U.$ Once again, we'll ask the question of whether $S\\in S{:}$\n\n- If $S\\in S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\notin S.$ But this is a contradiction.\n\n- If $S\\notin S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\in S.$ But this is also a contradiction.\n\nThus, to resolve the paradox, we're left with no choice but to conclude that $S\\not\\subseteq U.$ This indicates that something is fundamentally wrong with our definition of $S,$ and no such set can exist because if it were a set, it would belong to a universal set. \n\n* If [math]S\\notin S,[/math] then by the definition of [math]S[/math] and applying De Morgan's law for conjunctions, we have\n\\begin{align*}\nS\\notin S \\Leftrightarrow \\lnot (S\\subseteq U\\land  S\\notin S)  \\equiv (S\\not\\subseteq U) \\lor (S\\in S).\n\\end{align*}" {:db/id 17592186055558 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056056 :tutorial/content "Recall that the natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and real and complex numbers can be arranged in the a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{Q},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{R},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{C}.$ We can write this symbolically as follows:\n\n$$\n\\mathbb{N} \\subseteq \\mathbb{Z} \\subseteq \\mathbb{Q} \\subseteq \\mathbb{R} \\subseteq \\mathbb{C}\n$$\n\nSince none of these sets are equivalent, we can also write\n\n$$\n\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z} \\subset \\mathbb{Q} \\subset \\mathbb{R} \\subset \\mathbb{C}.\n$$\n\nSome restricted or extended special sets are subsets of others. For example:\n\n- $\\mathbb N$ is the set of natural numbers, and $\\mathbb N_0$ is the set of natural numbers *and* zero. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\mathbb N\\subset \\mathbb N_0.\n$$\n\n- $\\mathbb Z$ is the set of integers, $\\mathbb Z^+$ is the set of positive integers (equivalent to $\\mathbb N$), and $\\mathbb Z^+_0$ is the set of positive integers and zero (equivalent to $\\mathbb N_0$). Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\mathbb Z^+\\subset  \\mathbb Z_0^+ \\subset \\mathbb Z.\n$$\n\n- $\\mathbb Q^+$ is the set of positive rational numbers, $\\mathbb R^+$ is the set of positive real numbers, and $\\mathbb R$ is the set of real numbers. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\mathbb Q^+\\subset  \\mathbb R^+ \\subset \\mathbb R.\n$$\n\nHowever, note that, for example, $\\mathbb Q \\not\\subset  \\mathbb R^+,$ since $0\\in\\mathbb Q$ yet $0\\notin \\mathbb R^+.$\n\nFrom these basic inclusions, we can now deduce some subset relationships for other special numerical sets. For example, recall that [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] represents the set of all non-negative integers. \n\n* Obviously, [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] is a proper subset of [math]\\mathbb{Z}[/math] since all the elements of [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] are integers but there are some integers, say, [math]-1,[/math] that does not belong to [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+.[/math] So, [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+ \\subset \\mathbb{Z}.[/math]\n\n* On the other hand, [math]\\mathbb{N}[/math] is a proper subset of [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] since all natural number lie in [math]\\mathbb{Z}_0^+[/math] but [math]0 \\notin \\mathbb{N}.[/math] So, [math]\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z}_0^+.[/math]\n\nTherefore, we have [math]\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z}_0^+ \\subset \\mathbb{Z}.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "c336106d-52a5-5d56-a98f-c64cd26eef4b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8317 :tutorial/title "Subsets of Special Sets"} :step/id #uuid "5386697a-6e4f-5619-83d7-53f1064c31f2" :step/math-academy-id 152767 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055559}} {:db/id 17592186056056 :tutorial/content "Recall that the natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and real and complex numbers can be arranged in the following hierarchical diagram.\n\n![](images/66/66260e4c239137cd30453d9335256fd7d84e93a197612d670c19d97e417bd2f0.png)\n\nIn other words, $\\mathbb{N}$ is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{Z},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{Q},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{R},$ which is a (proper) subset of $\\mathbb{C}.$ We can write this symbolically as follows:\n\n$$\n\\mathbb{N} \\subseteq \\mathbb{Z} \\subseteq \\mathbb{Q} \\subseteq \\mathbb{R} \\subseteq \\mathbb{C}\n$$\n\nSince none of these sets are equivalent, we can also write\n\n$$\n\\mathbb{N} \\subset \\mathbb{Z} \\subset \\mathbb{Q} \\subset \\mathbb{R} \\subset \\mathbb{C}.\n$$\n\nSome restricted or extended special sets are subsets of others. Can't we just let the universal set be the set of everything?\n\nThe answer is no. If we don't specify a well-defined universal set, we encounter a nonsensical situation called **Russell's paradox.**\n\nFirst, suppose there exists a set $\\Omega$ that contains absolutely everything, including every mathematical object, every thought, every book, every person, animal, cell, and star in the universe, past, present, or future. \n\nRussell's paradox originates from the following idea:\n\n> *Define $S$ as the set that contains all sets that are not elements of themselves.*\n> \n> \n> $$\n> S = \\{A\\in \\Omega\\,:\\, A\\notin A\\}\n> $$\n\nMost sets you can think of are elements of $S.$ For example, the set $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}$ is in $S$ because $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}\\notin \\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$ \n\nIt takes a bit of thought to find sets that *aren't* members of $S.$ Such sets do exist, although typical examples are somewhat abstract: \n\n- The set containing all possible sets.\n\n- The set containing all possible thoughts.\n\n- The set $X,$ given by\n\n$$\nX = \\Big\\{\\underbrace{\\big\\{ \\left\\{\\{\\ldots \\}\\right\\}\\big\\}}_{X}\\Big\\}.\n$$\n\nHowever, what about $S$ itself? Is $S$ an element of $S?$ There are only two possibilities:\n\n- If $S\\in S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\notin S.$ But this is a contradiction because we cannot have $S\\in S$ *and* $S\\notin S.$\n\n- If $S\\notin S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we must have that $S\\in S.$ But this leads to the same contradiction as before!\n\nThe only way to resolve this is to conclude that $S\\notin \\Omega,$ but this is also a contradiction since $\\Omega$ contains absolutely everything!  So, there is no consistent answer to the question of whether $S$ itself is an element of $S.$ This is Russell's paradox, and when it was discovered, it shook the foundations of mathematics to its very core.\n\nThe issue, unknown to mathematicians until later, is that the object [math]S[/math] is not a set. If it were, Russell's paradox would not occur since we should always be able to determine whether an object is a member of a set or not.\n\nLater, it was realized that if a set is defined using a predicate, we should ensure that all sets involved are subsets of some larger set $U$ (i.e., a universal set) where we can always determine which elements are members of $U$ and which are not, at least in principle.\n\nTo see how this resolves Russell's paradox, suppose $U$ is a universal set. Let's refine our definition of $S$ as follows:\n\n$$\nS = \\{A\\subseteq U\\,:\\,A\\notin A\\}\n$$\n\nWe'll assume $S$ is a set, so $S\\subseteq U$ for some well-defined $U.$ Once again, we'll ask the question of whether $S\\in S{:}$\n\n- If $S\\in S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\notin S.$ But this is a contradiction.\n\n- If $S\\notin S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\in S.$ But this is also a contradiction.\n\nThus, to resolve the paradox, we're left with no choice but to conclude that $S\\not\\subseteq U.$ This indicates that something is fundamentally wrong with our definition of $S,$ and no such set can exist because if it were a set, it would belong to a universal set. \n\n* If [math]S\\notin S,[/math] then by the definition of [math]S[/math] and applying De Morgan's law for conjunctions, we have\n\\begin{align*}\nS\\notin S \\Leftrightarrow \\lnot (S\\subseteq U\\land  S\\notin S)  \\equiv (S\\not\\subseteq U) \\lor (S\\in S).\n\\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "0e2d16c6-3382-5ba2-8d4b-949482eb4f07" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9388 :tutorial/title "Russell's Paradox: Why We Need a Universal Set"} :step/id #uuid "7280da1b-4410-550f-9a00-d46456526bfc" :step/math-academy-id 164820} {:db/id 17592186056075 :tutorial/content "You might wonder why we need to define a universal set. 17592186046941 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1005 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating strings, mechanical systems, and electromagnetic circuits." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1012 154 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1013 "PS1" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1014 #uuid continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.\nThe course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.\nStudents then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.\nApplications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.\nThe course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.\nStudents next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.\nApplications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.\nThe course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.\nLaplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.\nThe course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in statistical physics and experimental analysis." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1012 155 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1013 "PS2" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1014 #uuid For example:\n\n- $\\mathbb N$ is the set of natural numbers, and $\\mathbb N_0$ is the set of natural numbers *and* zero. Can't we just let the universal set be the set of everything?\n\nThe answer is no. If we don't specify a well-defined universal set, we encounter a nonsensical situation called **Russell's paradox.**\n\nFirst, suppose there exists a set $\\Omega$ that contains absolutely everything, including every mathematical object, every thought, every book, every person, animal, cell, and star in the universe, past, present, or future. \n\nRussell's paradox originates from the following idea:\n\n> *Define $S$ as the set that contains all sets that are not elements of themselves.*\n> \n> \n> $$\n> S = \\{A\\in \\Omega\\,:\\, A\\notin A\\}\n> $$\n\nMost sets you can think of are elements of $S.$ For example, the set $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}$ is in $S$ because $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}\\notin \\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$ \n\nIt takes a bit of thought to find sets that *aren't* members of $S.$ Such sets do exist, although typical examples are somewhat abstract: \n\n- The set containing all possible sets.\n\n- The set containing all possible thoughts.\n\n- The set $X,$ given by\n\n$$\nX = \\Big\\{\\underbrace{\\big\\{ \\left\\{\\{\\ldots \\}\\right\\}\\big\\}}_{X}\\Big\\}.\n$$\n\nHowever, what about $S$ itself? Is $S$ an element of $S?$ There are only two possibilities:\n\n- If $S\\in S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\notin S.$ But this is a contradiction because we cannot have $S\\in S$ *and* $S\\notin S.$\n\n- If $S\\notin S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we must have that $S\\in S.$ But this leads to the same contradiction as before!\n\nThe only way to resolve this is to conclude that $S\\notin \\Omega,$ but this is also a contradiction since $\\Omega$ contains absolutely everything!  So, there is no consistent answer to the question of whether $S$ itself is an element of $S.$ This is Russell's paradox, and when it was discovered, it shook the foundations of mathematics to its very core.\n\nThe issue, unknown to mathematicians until later, is that the object [math]S[/math] is not a set. If it were, Russell's paradox would not occur since we should always be able to determine whether an object is a member of a set or not.\n\nLater, it was realized that if a set is defined using a predicate, we should ensure that all sets involved are subsets of some larger set $U$ (i.e., a universal set) where we can always determine which elements are members of $U$ and which are not, at least in principle.\n\nTo see how this resolves Russell's paradox, suppose $U$ is a universal set. Let's refine our definition of $S$ as follows:\n\n$$\nS = \\{A\\subseteq U\\,:\\,A\\notin A\\}\n$$\n\nWe'll assume $S$ is a set, so $S\\subseteq U$ for some well-defined $U.$ Once again, we'll ask the question of whether $S\\in S{:}$\n\n- If $S\\in S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\notin S.$ But this is a contradiction.\n\n- If $S\\notin S,$ then by the definition of $S,$ we have that $S\\in S.$ But this is also a contradiction.\n\nThus, to resolve the paradox, we're left with no choice but to conclude that $S\\not\\subseteq U.$ This indicates that something is fundamentally wrong with our definition of $S,$ and no such set can exist because if it were a set, it would belong to a universal set. \n\n* If [math]S\\notin S,[/math] then by the definition of [math]S[/math] and
